subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF WAGE RESTRAINT PROGRAM TO STAFF OF MEMBERS AND SENATORS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. One thousand and twenty-five women and 247 men who make up the staff of MPs and Senators are to become the latest victims of the government's unjust society. The government amendment introduced last Friday to the wage restraint legislation, Bill C-124, treats staff members, who have no security or tenure, more harshly than it treats public servants or even members of this House. That the government immediately amend the legislation before us in Bill C-124 so that its provisions take effect for the staffs of MPs and Senators on the expiry of their present salary arrangements as they will for all employees in the public service, and that the staffs of MPs and Senators not be singled out for punitive action by the government.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ADOPTION OF SUNSET LAWS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Canadians are finally realizing that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is galloping us down the slippery slope to complete socialism. The energy minister for the British government, Mr. Nigel Lawson, is quoted as saying that this fall or winter when that government sells off its state-owned oil company to the private sector, "It will be the biggest new issue that the London Stock Exchange has ever seen." The British government will sell 51 per cent to the public. Hurrah for the mother of democracy!
At a time when other governments-Britain and the U.S. are notable examples-are selling off state enterprises, Socialist Liberal Canada is adding to the total of more money-losing Crown corporations. Whereas privatization means more competition, lower prices to the consumer, badly needed injections of cash for government, a smaller bureaucracy, and a larger stake for Canadians in their country, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor):
That the government immediately embrace sunset laws and make the average Canadian a true partner by stock offerings in various of the 480 Crown agencies. Petro-Canada would be a significant first step in tipping the balance back to the private sector. If it's ours, make it ours.

speechtext:

Underlying this, and the inability of the Canadian government to respond properly to this economic crisis, is the fact that we have a degree of foreign ownership in Canada which is higher than any other industrialized nation would permit. Many Canadian businesses have gone under; others have cut management and workers' salaries. But favourites of the government in a Liberal stronghold are not required to trim fat. Favourite son treatment and preferential loans are assured. Therefore, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer):
That if the government is serious about the 6 per cent society it hopes to create, it review and slash its own runaway spending and cease its huge payouts to Liberal Party golden-haired businesses.

subsubtopic: PERMISSION SOUGHT TO USE IMPERIAL AND METRIC MEASUREMENTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canada's push toward metric has been unnecessary and costly for farmers, as well as exceedingly frustrating. Now it is resulting in expensive crop losses and possible environmental hazards because of major mistakes in chemical formulations given in the new metric books and pamphlets. For example, a loss of 200 acres of dead alfalfa was reported in the weekend news. Under imperial measures farmers could spot such errors which often are typographical, but the strange metric language makes this almost impossible. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass):
That manufacturers and processors be permitted to include imperial as well as metric measurements and instructions on their product labels and books.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. speechtext: Madam Speaker, I suppose that that is a question of judgment and the hon. member has already expressed his views, as did another member of his party, on Friday, I believe. But in the view of this government, since this company had plans for recovery which were judged to be acceptable and plausible by the banks and the government, it was important to try to give them assistance. subtopic: SUNCOR CORPORATION-DEFINITION OF HISTORICAL PROFIT MARGINS
SUNCOR CORPORATION-DEFINITION OF HISTORICAL PROFIT MARGINS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The minister will probably recall that on Tuesday last, in a statement issued by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources with regard to Suncor, it was stated that the company has also committed itself to supporting federal wage guidelines of 6 per cent and 5 per cent and-this is the part with which I want to deal-will limit increases of prices not subject to the energy agreement with Alberta to levels that are consistent with the lower rates of interest and costs and restoration of historical profit margins.
On the weekend, Leonard Good, the director general in the federal Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, said that he simply did not know the implications of this statement in terms of its legality or monitoring, or in deciding the definition of "historical profit margins." Since it is the Minister of Finance who will have to decide what historical profit margins are, and given that this is the first in a whole series of what I suspect will be attempts by companies to restore what they consider to be historical profit margins, what is the definition that the government intends to apply to the term "historical profit margins?"

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: SUNCOR CORPORATION-DEFINITION OF HISTORICAL PROFIT MARGINS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 have not seen the quote that is attributed to Mr. Good in terms of the commitment given by Suncor. It has been spelled out in a press release and, as my hon. friend has indicated, the government will follow the evolution of prices. We have not introduced a system of price controls any more than we have instituted a system of wage controls of a general nature. We have asked for the voluntary co-operation of industry, of the private sector and of the unions.
In this particular instance, the company has volunteered to adhere to the wage guidelines which the government has imposed upon itself. It has also volunteered to keep its price increases to a minimum level, bearing in mind the factors to which the hon. member has referred. We are operating on the basis of a voluntary commitment system. We will examine how the company behaves as time goes on, under this voluntary commitment. I remind the hon. member that the government has not introduced a system of wage and price controls in the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT AFFECTING WAGES OF LEGISLATORS' STAFFS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. On Friday last the minister gave notice that he intends actually to cut the pay of staffs of Members of Parliament and senators, 80 per cent of whom are women. These staffs are denied free collective bargaining rights and, in many instances, are certainly not overpaid. In view of the fact that this sleazy, shameful move, which constitutes nothing less than playing cheap politics on the backs of hard-working parliamentary staff members, puts this group of employees in a worse position than any other employees in the country, including Members of Parliament and senators, will the minister explain this shameful betrayal of our employees, and will be reconsider this shabby scapegoating amendment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT AFFECTING WAGES OF LEGISLATORS' STAFFS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the accusation is somewhat exaggerated. If I may take a moment, let me explain why this amendment was judged to be necessary. Hon. members may recall that the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, supported by the hon. member for Perth and the hon. member for Peterborough, accused the government of treating ministerial exempt staff with undue favour by providing a 10 per cent raise which was decided May 13. When I look at Hansard, I see that the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton said on July 5:
-why does he-
He was referring to me.
-not do the honourable thing and roll them all back so that the exempt staff will stand in exactly the same position as public servants?
In fact, exempt staff did stand in exactly the same position as public servants, but to a degree the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton apparently was successful in misleading the country and independent observers into thinking some favouritism had been granted.
It is absolutely fundamental to the credibility of this program that the government be perceived as dealing harshly with Members of Parliament, with itself, and with others. Thanks to the efforts of the opposition, that has become virtually impossible in the present circumstances, and hence it is with some regret-but, nevertheless, judged to be necessary-that we put all political appointees, in keeping with the request of the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, on the same footing.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. The minister has broken the solemn promise he made to this House on July 9 when he said there would be no reductions in wages and salaries for anyone other than Members of Parliament and senators. The minister stated, in reply to representations made by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, that he would not make ministerial staffs, as he put it, "particular sacrificial lambs." How can the minister stand before us with any sense of equity or fairness and say he intends to make this particular
group of employees the victims of his game of political one-upmanship with the Conservative Party? Will the minister now stop trying to score cheap political points on the backs of the staffs of Members of Parliament and senators?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are not talking about political points. We are talking about a national assault on inflation, with the federal government taking the lead.
Because of accusations that have been made which, on their face and on the facts, are false, a number of observers such as the Ottawa Citizen last week, a respected newspaper in this country, wrote that:
Another example of its bankruptcy-
Speaking of the government-
-came when Liberal MPs defeated a Tory effort to have cabinet aides' salaries cut back to the 6 per cent guideline, along with public servants.
Clearly, even the editorial staff of the Ottawa Citizen was misled by the statements coming from the member for Nepean-Carleton. Not only that, they refer to 11 per cent, but the next day, I should point out, there was an apology in the newspaper pointing out that the figure was 10 per cent. So there is no effort here at all to take advantage or to score cheap political points.
What is important is that the government be perceived as taking the lead and that it not be accused falsely by members of the opposition. It is with regret that I introduced this amendment, but in the circumstances it is clearly necessary if the public has the impression that political appointees were enjoying some special benefit.

He said: Madam Speaker, I believe the time has come to move expeditiously to the conclusion of report stage and third reading of Bill C-124.
First, let me say that the proceedings to date have been fruitful, that the work of committee members on all sides of the House has been productive, has brought forward change and comment, and that we now have before us a number of additional motions which appear on the Order Paper, some of which were discussed briefly on Friday and a number of which, I hope, we will have the opportunity of debating during the closing hours of report stage. I would point out that in the

August 2, 1982
Time Allocation
course of the debate before the committee a number of significant amendments were made. In addition, of course, we have the further amendments on the Order Paper to which I made reference.
Let me, if I may, for just a moment touch upon those to remind the House where major progress has been made in improving the bill and in making it more effective in achieving its ends and also more equitable in its application. 1 refer the House to the change in Clause 3, subparagraph (4), which has the effect of extending the application of the bill to employees of Canadian Pacific Limited and its subsidiaries as well as to the employees of a number of other railway companies which are specifically enumerated, namely the Ontario Northland Railway, the Algoma Central Railway Company, Toronto Terminals Railway Company and Shawinigan Falls Terminal Railway Company.
Members will recall that these amendments were brought about because of the history and importance attached to joint bargaining by both the unions, on the one hand, and by management on the other. This joint bargaining has a history of something like ninety years, and with this amendment which was introduced at committee stage that joint bargaining, that very important institution, will be preserved.
In addition, much has been said during the course of this debate with respect to the issue of collective bargaining and the importance of continuing a measure of collective bargaining during the period of this wage restraint program. At the committee stage I introduced an amendment which is now found in Clause 7 of the bill. That amendment goes some way to restoring and preserving collective bargaining in that it permits parties to a collective agreement which has been extended in accordance with the terms and conditions of the act to amend by agreement any terms or conditions of the collective agreement or arbitral award other than wage rates or other terms and conditions of the compensation plan.
This means with respect to those non-monetary items-and I think particularly of the issue of health and safety which is of concern I know to all members of this House, to members of management and to members of the unions themselves-that they will be permitted during the extension of any agreement under the provisions of the law to continue to collectively bargain and to agree on these very important areas.
There stands on the Order Paper further amendments dealing with the issue of collective bargaining. There is a proposed amendment standing in the name of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), and I hope in the time remaining to us we will have the opportunity of exchanging our views with respect to the proposed application of that amendment. That stands as Motion No. 9.
1 suggest-and I will elaborate on this a good deal further in the course of debate at report stage-that this amendment in fact falls far short of what the member for Rosedale himself seeks to achieve in terms of preserving and enhancing the collective bargaining process. At the same time 1 will have the
opportunity to elaborate at some length on Motion No. 17 standing in the name of the President of the Treasury Board, which provides that the governor in council may by order terminate the application of this act in respect of an employee or group of employees to which this act applies.
That, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, is a very significant amendment in terms of the preservation of the collective bargaining system. I indicated in this House and in a release which I made at the time this amendment was tabled that this amendment will permit parties who would otherwise be bound by this agreement to enter into negotiations and to arrive at an agreement through the application of the traditional collective bargaining process, subject to the 6 per cent and 5 per cent total limit. This means that within that limit parties will be able to negotiate, to make trade-offs, to permit items such as, for example, maternity leave, which was raised by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) in the course of the debate at the committee stage, to be incorporated into collective agreements and then, when the parties have reached an agreement, they will be subject to order by the governor in council, an order which will in fact terminate the application of the law with respect to that particular contract, with respect to that employer and with respect to that group of employees.
I see this amendment as being very significant. I realize I have only a few minutes to speak on the motion and hence I do not intend to engage in a wide and complete analysis of how that particular provision can be applied as opposed to how the proposed amendment of the hon. member for Rosedale will be applied. However, I suggest that this permits maximum flexibility to take account of the wide variety of circumstances that can exist with respect to any particular employee or group of employees and permit agreement to be reached through the normal operation of the collective bargaining process, subject at all times to the over-all limitation of 6 per cent and 5 per cent which, of course, is fundamental to the thrust of this wage restraint program.
We have already discussed at some length motion No. 3. It was the subject of some exchange in the House during question period. As I indicated during my comments on Friday, I regret that this amendment is necessary but I believe that in the circumstances, due to the unfortunate impression that has been created across this country and has been adopted by some observers in the media to the effect that one particular group has been singled out for favoured treatment, it was the government's decision, to counter what I call that unfortunate impression, that all political appointees in fairness must be treated on the same footing.
I know that comments have been made. We heard them on Friday, we heard them during question period. We know the effect is to treat these employees in a way which is more difficult for them than any other group of employees to which the bill applies. We know that, but we ask them also as good public servants to join with us in this anti-inflation crusade and set an example which all Canadians are being asked to follow.

One indeed wonders whether the average Canadian realizes that one dollar out of every four dollars spent by the federal government is now spent on interest and debt charges-it is more like "depth charges", for it indeed will surely sink us.
The former Auditor General, James Macdonell, predicts that the deficit will reach $22.5 billion for this year. That is $3 billion more than the government estimate. This Liberal government is trying to hide its own responsibilities by blaming all of our economic problems on American policy.
As Barbara Amiel stated in the Sun on July 11, 1982, "Reagan has cut taxes; Trudeau increased them. Reagan has cut government programs; Trudeau is increasing them. Reagan is trying to cut the deficit; Trudeau has doubled it. The United States is importing less oil; Canada's oil costs are going up."

This land was settled and developed into the great country that it is today by our forefathers who came here to overcome the odds, try new things and accomplish goals unobtainable in the old world, for we are not at the mercy of the world. The Progressive Conservative Party believes in the Canadian people and the great future of our country. Today, Canada is at a crossroads both in government policy and lack in confidence of the Canadian people as a result of the political, social and economic system. speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak once again on Bill C-124 because I support it wholeheartedly. People in my riding, and people I have met across Canada since the budget, overwhelmingly support the idea that 6 per cent and 5 per cent are manageable economic targets and manageable ways to bring our economy back to recovery.
Bill C-124 provides leadership by asking public servants and politicians to limit their salary increases to 6 per cent and 5 per cent over the next two years. More important, this bill stands as a symbol of the necessary collective effort that all of us must put into our recovery. Let us repeat over and over again that 6 per cent is a manageable target, 6 per cent is an increase

August 2, 1982
Time Allocation
that will bring health to our economy, 6 per cent is something that each person in our society can contribute to our mutual recovery.
Inflation is the economic disease that all of us can help defeat. We cannot reach out into our traditional markets around the world and into other economies to change their direction, but we can fix our own economy and bring it under control so that when the world recovery comes, we will be there to take advantage of it.
This bill limiting wage increases in the federal public service provides only the first step toward that recovery. It is the example to the rest of our society. We as an employer are saying to our employees that we will go through this step. However, we are asking the rest of our economy to come along with us.
We just heard a very passionate speech from the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) on prices and profits. He raises a question that many people ask. Are they going to go through limited wage increases only to see unconscionable increases on the price side? Quite fairly and quite rightly, ordinary people are asking this question.
I wish to refer to today's Globe and Mail "Report on Business". The lead article on that page is entitled "Industry prices tumble in weak economy". It states that the industry price selling index for June was 6.5 per cent. I quote from the article to explain why this is happening:
The selling price index provides a hopeful sign that inflation is slackening and that consumer prices are likely to be on a downward trend. During the last period when manufacturers were being forced to limit prices increases, in the spring of 1977, retail prices moved down markedly-
The small advance in manufactured goods prices also gives credence to the view that the government's restraint measures are unnecessary in the case of most private sector companies.
In the private sector we are seeing a slowdown in some prices. What we are also seeing as a result of the government's action following the budget is a slowdown in government administered prices. We are seeing some very tough leadership on the part of individual ministers and the cabinet collectively to control prices that we influence. We are seeing the price side slow down because of the influence of our economy and the leadership of the federal government.
Personally, I welcome the enthusiasm that 1 heard from the mayors of Canada's leading municipalities last week when they talked about influencing prices in their local situation. I welcome as well the initiative taken by the province of British Columbia to join in the 6-5 plan, because that will affect the wages and administered prices in that province. I hope that other provinces from Alberta to Newfoundland will join British Columbia in this effort. Whether it be rent controls or beer in the ballpark, we need 6 per cent and 5 per cent in prices as much as we do in wages. We would welcome the involvement of the provinces to help us with that.
Turning back to the bill and the question of the increases that we are extending to public servants, I am reminded of a conversation I had last Friday at the Ottawa airport with the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie). On Friday we had a very heated debate here, and that debate carried over when the two of us met on the weekend. We were discussing whether
the 6 per cent rule could be fairly applied to people on the lower pay scales in the public service.
After a few minutes we were interrupted by a total stranger who introduced himself as an Ottawa area businessman. He told us that his experience was that he could not keep a typist on his payroll because that person would be so highly paid in the public service. Following that experience, I thought about my own riding. I realized that the men and women who work at the Gateway postal station are some of the highest paid industrial workers in my riding, and my riding is a very affluent area.
These two examples show why our leadership is badly needed in this area. We have good workers. We have given them honest rates of pay. They have bargained fairly for those rates of pay. Today the outside world is influenced very directly by the pay we give our employees. Our leadership is vital. Despite the comments we just heard a few moments ago, we must recognize that our employees receive very good salaries and have very good job security. We must realize that in those circumstances our employees can limit their increases over the next two years and provide the leadership that is so badly needed.
Today we must remember as well that that leadership will be hollow if we cannot encourage other employees and employers across this country to join in. We must convince Canadians that this is a collective and manageable effort. We are asking our employees to show the way, but we are asking the rest of the country to follow. Their support will be vital.
I appreciate the opportunity to join in the debate today. I hope this bill will pass quickly through the House. I know the people in my riding, the people on the radio shows and those in the cities across this country with whom I have spoken in the last month support this initiative. They are ready to follow our leadership. They believe us when we say that together we can reach a 6 per cent world and that in a 6 per cent world we are in a position to recover our economic health. In a 6 per cent world we will be ready to join the recovery of the whole world when that recovery comes. We need a joint effort.
I thank our public servants and I thank those in our Crown corporations for helping us to provide that leadership for the rest of our economy.

I want to say at the outset of this debate that I oppose the way Standing Order 75 is being used, and the motion before us is a perfect example of my point. The House of Commons is a debating forum. Its purpose is to bring forward, from the government and the opposition, points of view on legislation before the House. If a matter before the House is complex and is the cause of concern and controversy in the country, the hon. members are required to convey those concerns in the House in debate. If a member is on the government side, he tends to look upon all remarks by opposition members as obstruction, as a means of stringing out the process and as a means of fouling the government's legislative timetable. On the other hand, opposition members many times must wrestle with legislative language that is obscure, which in many cases requires considerable research, which is poorly drafted, with loopholes through which one could drive a Mack truck and which is based on wrong-headed, immature and biased information and opinion, as we see in Bill C-124 and Bill C-53, to name two current bills.
Standing Order 75C was placed in our House business procedures to allow the government to bring to an end a debate which had run beyond a reasonable time. It was not intended that a complex bill be entered on the Order Paper and scheduled for debate and, within two hours, time allocation placed on that bill. That is using the rule book as a sledgehammer.
There is no reason in the world why the House of Commons cannot work to a proper legislative timetable. There should be a set timetable for the House to convene, a period of recess for Christmas and New Year's, a short break at Easter and a predetermined recess date. It then becomes the government's problem to fit its legislative program into that time-frame. There would have to be provision for emergencies which require parliamentary action. Anyone who examines the process presently in use has to agree that the quality of debate would be vastly improved if we had to work to a parliamentary time schedule.
Having said that, let me deal with the matter at hand. The government introduced Bill C-124, which has a wide and sweeping effect on the economy. Even before the bill has passed, we are being told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the PMO that if this bill does not work, then full wage and price controls will be legislated. The Prime Minister has even gone further, stating that if the provisions of Bill C-124 fail and wage and price controls fail, then the economy will collapse.
The truth of the matter is that one picture is painted by legislation-Bill C-124-and another by the Prime Minister. A third picture is presented to business and labour leaders when they meet behind cabinet doors with the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and his officials. In other words, we have an economic situation that is bad news, very bad news and potential economic disaster. The longer we stay here and debate, the more likely it is that those "private
Time Allocation
details," spoken about only behind doors with selected groups, will become public knowledge.
As hon. members know, the budget forecasts a deficit of $19.6 billion, but the deficit is based on a turnaround in the economy in the third and fourth quarters. No one in the private sector with whom I have talked has forecast a bottoming out or a turnaround for at least 18 months. The question which begs to be asked is, what will the deficit be if there is no turnaround in the third and fourth quarters? I believe information is being given to those persons meeting with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance which is not intended for the public.
It has been speculated that the deficit could climb to $25 billion or $28 billion. If that proves to be true, we could face economic collapse. I hope that speculation remains only speculation and that the provisions of Bill C-124 are adequate to bring some order to a deteriorating economy. However, I do not believe the people of Canada are being well served when the truth of the gravity of the situation we face is held from them.
When the Prime Minister states that the people of Canada demanded high interest rates and that is why the government had to pay 19.5 per cent interest on Canada Savings Bonds, I believe that is an abuse of the truth. Equally, when the government, through the Prime Minister, intervenes in the market process through regulations designed as fine tuning and then declares that the enterprise system is not working, that also is an abuse of the truth. When the government refuses to curb its own expenditures, through sleight-of-hand rhetoric states it is curbing employment and then hires an additional 8,000 people in the first quarter on this year, that is deception which borders on contempt. When the government blames wage demands on labour as the cause of inflation when in fact it is a reaction to inflation, that is bending the truth and inflaming an already precarious situation.
It is because the government is firmly committed to intervening continually in the marketplace and believes it can only spend its way out of inflation that we will continue to have difficulties. Had the government dealt directly with those problems in the last few months, then perhaps we would be recessing this House on a positive note and a plan would be in place to alleviate the economic difficulties we face. But that is not the case. Instead, we are presented with a poorly drafted bill, the scope of which keeps changing with each succeeding question period. For these reasons, I oppose the imposition of Standing Order 75C in this debate.

I have just spent 15 days in committee, considering Bill C-124. One party, the New Democratic Party, told us at the beginning: well, we do not know whether there are going to be any amendments. We are going to have a caucus meeting this week and then we will be able to tell you. They had a caucus meeting, they came back and said well, we still do not know whether we are going to have any amendments. We will know after the next caucus meeting. A week later, there was another caucus meeting, with the same results. However, there was a possibility, and we finally received the amendments in committee, although it was like pulling eye teeth. Another example, when the same party, the New Democratic Party, wanted to invite witnesses to appear before the committee, instead of just presenting a motion requesting that people appear before the committee, they presented about five of these motions, which we had to vote down, one by one. Just one more way to make us waste an hour of our time. It is so ridiculous, Mr. Speaker, because while we on the government side are being kept here in the House, we cannot see our constituents who would like to meet with us to discuss their problems.
The opposition parties usually keep half of their members here, and it is high time Canadians realized that, while we have to be here to support our policies, those people are using delaying tactics and are strutting around their ridings, playing politics. Where was the member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), the Leader of the New Democratic Party during the first week Bill C-124 was considered in committee? I do not know, but he was not in Parliament, either at the committee meetings or in the House. That is what we have to put up with, Mr. Speaker. We are asked to come to Ottawa to represent 80,000 or 90,000 people and to sit in Parliament from the middle of October until the begining of August and probably until the middle of August, five days a week. Mr. Speaker, we are told to be there, because the opposition might call a vote. For instance, the bells crisis which cost us 15 days. And then we are criticized for
using solutions like Standing Order 75C. No, I feel we must act sensibly, and I think Canadians realize this. I am not particularly happy about the fact that, as the member for Lac-Saint-Jean, I am going to vote to have salary increases of public servants restricted to 6 and 5 per cent. No one likes to do that. I would much rather give them 20 per cent a year!
Nor am I particularly happy about the fact that I voted for a cut in my own salary of over $3,000, just for this year, plus a cut in our special member's allowance. Nobody likes to do that either. But it has to be done, Mr. Speaker. It has to be done on behalf of thousands of unemployed workers who are waiting for inflation to go down. It has to be done on behalf of the taxpayer, because, and many people are unaware of this in this House, Quebec taxpayers are literally being squeezed dry by the PQ, as the member for Laval (Mr. Roy) has said, and if no one eases their burden, they will go under. Meanwhile, the New Democratic Party is setting itself up as the defender of I forget what it was.
I was listening to them in committee. The CLC branch plant, Mr. Speaker! And the CLC is not even a political party! If only they were speaking for the workers, but none of these people has realized Canadian workers think that they are paying too many taxes, that government spending is perhaps a bit too high, that federal buildings are perhaps a bit too big and a bit too air-conditioned and too luxurious. None of these people has realized that Canadians feel that perhaps we have too many public servants, because in ten years' time, the Liberal government has doubled the number of public employees. Mr. Speaker, those people are defending Mr. McDermott in committee, and meanwhile, people in their ridings and ours are unemployed. Do they go back to see them? No! Do not ask them what is going on in their ridings, they do not even know! They do not want to know because they are not interested. The only thing that interests them is what Mr. McDermott can deliver. It was incredible, Mr. Speaker, but at the same committee, the briefing notes that were handed out to the New Democratic Party had been prepared by the union representatives sitting there. That is really incredible. And meanwhile, their party leader was travelling around. Where, I do not know, but he was travelling. I believe in being sincere and honest with Canadians. Our country is experiencing financial problems.
The Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that what Japan and what West Germany have done, we can do here in Canada. But we need everyone's help. We have started by setting an example ourselves. The New Democratic Party should stop being a branch plant, it should present positive ideas that will contribute to the wellbeing of Canadians and not to the wellbeing of the privileged classes who have comfortable jobs with fat pay cheques for life. Mr. Speaker, I listened with some interest to what the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Gimaiel) had to say. One of his comments concerned the urgent need that he felt to be out of here and that the opposition parties were holding up the recess of the House of Commons. He said that he wanted to get back to his constituency. I 'can understand that desire on his part. I know that a lot of members would like to be working in their own constituencies. But I want to tell the hon. member that the opposition parties are not holding up the recess of the House. The people holding up the recess of the House, as far as I, as the member for Kingston and the Islands, am concerned, are the government members who will not bring in Bill C-53, the amendments to the Criminal Code, which will allow us to change the crime of rape to a series of sexual assault charges. As long as that bill is not brought into the House I am not going home, and I want him to know that. That bill has to come before the House before we recess for the summer.
I am very interested in the fact that the government feels it necessary at this point to introduce a motion under Standing Order 75C on Bill C-124. This is a bill which the government said is key to its economic recovery plan and is one of the major pieces of legislation introduced in this session. What I find very unusual about the government's use of closure is that it always feels it is necessary to use it on the major pieces of legislation it brings into the House, the things that it considers to be most important and which should justify the greatest examination by members on all sides and members of the committee. Before that can take place the government brings in closure and cuts off debate. It moved closure on the Constitution bill before it was even under way. Before the country knew what was happening with regard to the major changes to the Constitution, the government introduced closure. And it has done so again.
What this signifies to me is that when it comes to major pieces of legislation that the government wants to introduce, it immediately feels insecure. The only thing it feels secure about is a motion under Standing Order 75C. It can hide behind closure instead of facing the legitimate questions that should be asked by its own party, by members of the opposition and by the Canadian public. That is the situation with this bill.
This bill requires a great deal of examination, Mr. Speaker. We have given it a fair amount of examination in committee but by no means have all the questions been answered. I very much regret the decision of the government to cut off debate before it has made its position clear with regard to its intentions on all aspects of the bill.
It seems that at every step of this bill the government has introduced new and ill-conceived amendments that have not been properly thought through. That was very evident in the House today when questions were put to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) about the 6 and 5 per cent society that he predicts, of which he says this bill is the cornerstone. What happened? He said, "Why are you asking me those questions? They concern somebody else. I should not

have to answer them." Surely if he is co-ordinating a program for the government he ought to be able to answer legitimate questions about to whom these 6-5 measures will apply and how far they will go. They have not been answered. That is why extra debating time is necessary.
I mentioned that he brings in ill-conceived amendments. Nothing is more ill conceived, as I pointed out to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) the other day, than Motion No. 3 standing in his own name. This is the amendment which changes the time period in which the restraint measures will apply to staff of Members of Parliament and members of the Senate. To that effect, I moved a motion today which I sincerely hope the President of the Treasury Board will consider. I asked that the government amend immediately Bill C-124 so that its provisions take effect for the staff of MPs and senators on the expiry of their present salary arrangements, as they will for all other employees in the public service, and that staff of MPs and senators not be singled out for punitive action by this government.
I listened to the President of the Treasury Board speak to that item when he took part in this closure debate. I made a note of some of the words he used when he spoke. He said "We have to take that step." In other words, to take the punitive action it has against the staff of Members of Parliament and senators in order to counter the unfortunate impression the government has received about the country with regard to another group of employees known as exempt ministerial staff. If the President of the Treasury Board were honest in his presentation, he would have stood in his place and said that exempt staff for ministers, on average, are paid much, much higher salaries than are staff of Members of Parliament and senators, who are in categories ranging from $24,000 a year down. Some of them earn as little as $14,000. The majority of them are women, many of whom, if the minsiter would take the time to inquire around this building, are single parents supporting families and who really should not be put in a situation where they are singled out for punitive action.
1 am sure that if the minister had asked a number of Members of Parliament whether we would have been willing to take a further cut so staff in our offices did not have to take a cut, he would have got agreement. I am sure he would have found that there were members willing to make that sacrifice so that the people unable to bear that kind of burden would not have had to. Those who follow parliamentary procedure a bit will know that time allocation is used in the Mother of Parliaments practically on a daily basis, and is a normal procedure appended to most bills. It is not as if we are pulling off some kind of a hijacking, something to which the hon. member's party is accustomed.
Dealing with the particular motion before us at this time, Mr. Speaker, I want to point out some articles in favour of it. There is a saying that a picture is worth a thousand words. I recall having seen a graph in The Financial Post about two months ago which compared the increase in wages in Canada over the past ten years to the increase in productivity. In that one graph was an excellent example of the ills afflicting our economy. Between 1971 and 1981 the increase in wages was something in the order of 157 per cent, whereas productivity had increased in that period by something like 5 per cent. A better illustration of our problems could not be provided.
Another factor glossed over frequently by the opposition parties is that 30 per cent of our gross national product is exported. This is a fabulous figure when compared with countries such as Japan and Germany which export only about 10 per cent of their gross national product. It demonstrates the extent to which Canada is dependent upon world markets for its prosperity and the extent to which we must be competitive in order to have continued growth and prosperity. For those who feel that perhaps a large part of our exports is in primary resources, I point out that it is more like 70 per cent which are in manufactured or semi-manufactured products. Therefore, it is clear that wage increases in Canada must be tied to productivity or we will be unable to compete with other countries.
Earlier this year I had the opportunity of talking to Sylvia Ostry, the former head of the Economic Council of Canada and now chief economist of OECD. She had been to West Germany, and she explained how its metalworkers' union settled in the neighbourhood of 4 per cent. It is the strongest union in that country and leads off bargaining for other sectors of the economy. Mrs. Ostry went into a bank and congratulated the bankers for this settlement. They sort of turned up their noses and said, "Yes, it is pretty good, but it could be better." She also explained that West German unions were realistic in their wage demands. They understood that Germany, in order to compete, had to have wage increases which matched increases in productivity. Also she explained that they were very well informed. Apparently most of the unions in West Germany have economists and other experts tied to their staffs or working for them, which enables them to embark upon negotiations in a very sensitive and intelligent matter. With the recent meetings of the government, the private sector and

Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased to have the opportunity to join in this segment of the discussion on Bill C-124. One thing which came to mind as I listened to some of the discussion so far on this bill was Murphy's law. Murphy's law suggests that if anything can go wrong, it will. The corollary of that, which comes from the discussion here and in committee, is Johnston's law; Johnston's law suggests that Murphy's law is optimistic.
There are many things wrong in terms of what we are doing here today in discussing the limitation of debate on Bill C-124. The bill embodies much of the principle of the government's 65 formula. I guess all Canadians can be very thankful that the government is now working with numbers which it can handle. Clearly the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) could not cope with tens and twenties because in a six-month period he made a $10 billion error in the deficit. Now we have him down to numbers which he can perhaps handle by using his digits and keeping everything straight. We are thankful for that initiative, but there are many flaws in the bill.
We have heard other hon. members mention that this was an ad hoc piece of legislation. There have been so many changes in such a short period of time that it has been very difficult for hon. members on all sides of the House to cope with the bill. Clearly the minister, by accepting some of the changes almost on a daily basis, has admitted that the bill is both imperfect and requires amendment and further change.
One area about which our party is concerned and would like to see changes in is the expression of the minister concerning contracts. In committee we suggested an amendment to look at how the 6-5 regime would apply to service contracts of the government. The professional contracts let by government are very major components in government spending. In fact, it is a $1 billion component. The amendment we suggested would have struck out some lines in the appropriate place, substituted therefor "or rate of pay", and would have included "any person engaged under personal service contracts".
In response to representations by our party in an attempt to include that very significant amendment which would indicate the true intentions of the government and its commitment to this principle, the minister said he would look at it and think about it. He has really come forward now with his most recent amendment, going after the staff of Members of Parliament and hitting people who are not the cause of the problem. These
Time Allocation
people are almost helpless bystanders in the situation. He has not presented today or at any other time any explanation of what he intends to do about a major sector over which he clearly has control and could do something about. We are very disappointed, but it is just one example of the kind of imperfect legislation which we have not yet had a full opportunity to examine.
There are many other things wrong with the whole scene. One matter which came to mind as I was sitting in committee listening to the discussions and some of the interventions, and again today in the House, was that the bill has holes through which one could drive a Maislin truck. The whole environment is clearly wrong. Again we will be limited in our ability to look at it. This is the kind of wrongness I should like to discuss.
We really have a political program which is trying to cope with the government's position in the Gallup poll, and with the obvious lack of support in the country for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), as expressed by repeated polls, whether Gallup or others. It is taking one piece of the problem created by the government and is trying to use it in a political way with a lot of imagery and a lot of political reaction to try to co-opt people in labour and in business, indeed people across the country who are concerned about the unemployment level, the 1.3 million declared and the many undeclared unemployed people, to alert them to the growing problems of businesses in Canada through the loss of liquidity and the difficulties they will be facing if they do not come to the point very quickly where they can do economic planning on the basis of interest rates which are 12 per cent or less. We have this entire country concerned about these things, and what we have is a political reaction, an effort on the part of the government to try to gain support of all these segments in order to deal with the problem they have created themselves.
I think on that basis alone people should question whether or not there is a program that justifies their support for this initiative. There should be, and this indeed is part of the problem. But where is the rest of that program? What other measures are going to be taken? Are we going to see the commitment that has been made to control prices fulfilled? Are we going to get other things done which would help restore investor confidence? Are we going to get things done that would give people the sense that the government is truly committed, as this party is, to restraint.
I do not see it in anything that has been brought forward so far. We still have many instances where we have aircraft flights taking off to expensive parties; we have continued high levels of government advertising and on and on. We have the expansion of the government's budget into the seventies of billions of dollars. We have the interest rate payments of $13 billion in one year which is above the level of total government spending ten years ago. We have all these things which do not give anyone who takes a look at them any sense that there is a

Time Allocation
serious initiative on the part of the government to hold true to this principle of restraint. That is the bottom line if we are going to resolve these problems.
There was a report from the Economic Council of Canada that has been mentioned in this House several times. That report suggested that the government itself is responsible for an 18 per cent inflationary factor, whereas private enterprise, the rest of the economy, has been running along at about a 9 per cent inflation factor. With that kind of background I think it is clear that it is the entire government framework that is at fault.
I would like to make reference now to some of the comments made by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), the House leader of the New Democratic Party. One of the ironies of sitting in opposition now and listening to members of a different opposition party discuss things is the way that they like to link the things that this party will support with the things that the government is doing, things that we have supported and have stood for for years and years and years and now are being criticized because of our consistency by people like the member for Hamilton Mountain.
There is nothing inconsistent at all in our opposing the limitation of the full discussion of this very important bill in spite of the fact that we do support the principle of restraint that is embodied in parts of this bill, imperfect as it is.

First of all, I should point out to the House that, contrary to what the member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) said a few moments ago, that we are now dealing with C-124, we are not; we are dealing with the application of a motion under Standing Order 75C to limit debate on that very bill. I have been somewhat surprised at your generosity, Mr. Speaker, in allowing members to continue the ongoing debate on Bill C-124 and, having made a couple of procedural points, I will take note of your generosity and also join in the fray on the substance of Bill C-124, the government's restraint program.
In answer to the member for Kingston and the Islands, I think it should be emphasized-and my friend the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) made the point a few minutes ago-that it is very convenient for any opposition party to vote against the application of rule 75C of our Standing Orders, but when those opposition parties themselves have the responsibility of government they change their tune.
Obviously the New Democratic Party has never had that luxury and I doubt that they ever will, certainly not in my lifetime; but the Conservative Party were in office just for that brief, fleeting period in 1979, and as was pointed out by my friend from Laurier the House leader of the Conservative government at the time, who is sitting in the chamber this afternoon, my good friend the hon. member for Nepean-
Carleton (Mr. Baker), rose in his place, I think it was on November 20, 1979, and moved a motion under 75C on the mortgage tax deductibility bill of the Conservative government. I was not here at the time but I remember reading the House of Commons Debates, and he said "This is not closure; this is a more gentle form of closing off debate."
I think those people who are watching us on television and those here in the galleries today should not accept the argument made by the member for Kingston and the Islands. We are not closing off debate, using the very brutal instrument of Standing Order 33; we are allocating a further amount of time. This is done in other parliaments with some regularity, and I would submit, Mr. Speaker, that if we are to order our business in a better fashion in this place in the future, we are going to have to come to grips with some kind of a normal time allocation process.
The substance of the matter really is something that I suppose one could talk more than ten minutes on, but certainly in the last 18 months there has not been any other issue that has so captured the imagination of the people of my constituency than the government's crusade to limit inflation to 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent the second year. I think the members on the other side, if they go home and talk to their constituents over the summer period, will get perhaps a very rude message, which is that the public accept this program and are very happy to see that the government is taking the initiative and showing leadership on this particular issue.
The opposition has been yelling at us for the last 18 months, seeking a consensus to deal with Canada's economic problem. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) meets with labour leaders, municipal leaders and business leaders, he is seeking a consensus. But this is not consensus in terms of the opposition. They are advocating these meetings and, once we meet, they say we are using these people. It is co-option. You can see that rhetoric comes cheap in the House of Commons, and we have seen it this afternoon. The government is seeking a consensus in dealing with the very urgent problems facing the economy, but when we meet with these leaders we are accused of coopting them for purely partisan reasons.
Let us be honest. This country is in a grave economic crisis. The election campaign can be fought whenever the election comes, but I think the Canadian public are getting fed up with the spectre of the opposition every day fighting an ongoing election campaign. One can only suspect their motives, but people like Mr. Mulholland of the Bank of Nova Scotia, Mr. Sinclair of CP Investments, very eminent Canadians from the business community-these are people not identified with the Liberal Party; they are outstanding business leaders-realize that we have to put aside all this backbiting, all this nitpicking, all this political partisanship. Because this is destroying the country as much as the ongoing economic problems.

Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to hear the last Liberal speaker quoting another great Liberal leader, Mr. Lenin, saying that it is the prime responsibility of the opposition to come to the aid of the government. I do think the parallel exists somehow. It is the concept that this government has of democracy, that it is our responsibility to come to their defence rather than the responsibility of the government to come to Canadians with solutions to its own problems.
Earlier in this very short debate we heard it suggested by some Liberal backbenchers that the debate on Bill C-124, the public service wage restraint act, has prevented them from travelling to their ridings to meet their constituents and hear their views. That is not really the case. They are in a rush to pass this bill through the House of Commons because they want to go on vacation. That is the truth of the matter.
We no longer call this motion closure. This motion is now called time allocation, to use the vernacular of the House. What this really means is that time allocation sounds much more acceptable to the Liberal government than the term "closure". If the government were honest, instead of calling the motion time allocation or even closure, it would call it "the vacation rush measure", since they want to rush off to the beaches.
When one reviews the history of this bill, one sees that the minister responsible introduced it only on the last day of June. Once he introduced the bill and had it printed, he took nine days to bring it to the House for debate. He finally had the courage to introduce it on July 9. Less than one week later he introduced time allocation on that stage of the debate.
The following week the Liberal majority on the committee restricted the number of witnesses so that no further witnesses could appear before the committee. They would not let other union leaders or other business leaders come forward and explain their position on the bill.
I have a letter which was sent to the clerk of the committee. It is from the National Union of Provincial Government Employees and is signed by their president, John Fryer. In this letter he says:
On behalf of the 230,000-member National Union of Provincial Government Employees I am writing to express our disappointment at not being able to appear before the committee and present our views on Bill C-124.
What is interesting is that the government has always claimed that this bill was to apply not only to federal employees, but it wanted this bill to be copied by provincial

The second group in the line of fire, after the bill has dealt with the federal government employees, would be the provincial government employees, which group the Liberal majority on the committee would not allow to come forward to express their opinions on this legislation. Another person who the Liberal majority on the committee would not let come forward was their own Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia). When my colleague for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) asked over and over again to have the Minister of Labour explain his position on this bill, 1 wondered why he could not come. Why did the Liberal majority on that committee prevent him from appearing? I now have some information from a letter which the Minister of Labour wrote to The Globe and Mail prior to the bill being introduced. In the letter he says:
The right to strike is one of the important cornerstones of a free and democratic society-
He went on to say:
There is clearly room for greater co-operation between unions and employers, and Parliament has entrusted to Labour Canada-
His own department.
the responsibility for assisting in the development and maintenance of constructive relationships.
That is a quote from what the minister wrote and it was published.
The bill destroys the entire collective bargaining process. It allows the government to break contracts that it has already signed. It outlaws strikes and prevents binding arbitration for many workers.
The Minister of Labour, who is now sitting in his seat, has refused to come forward to explain how he can write one thing in a letter one day and then his government introduces a measure which does exactly the opposite a couple of weeks later. He has refused to do so with the compliance of the Liberal majority on the committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a proper place for closure. However, report stage of this bill is not the proper place. At report stage there were two NDP speakers, four Progressive Conservatives and one Liberal. It is not the time for closure or time allocation when we have not yet even started to cover the subject, let alone repeat ourselves.
The hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) made much ado about the people of Canada wanting restraint. He is right. However, he said they want nothing more than restraint, and I do not agree. There is something more the people want, and that is the resignation of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Liberal government. The vast majority of the people in this country want that even more than restraint. In any other country, the Prime Minister would have resigned long ago. He would have been impeached for the policies he has brought in. The national energy policy helped push the country down the tube. The November 12 budget pushed it even further. That is what started the depression in Canada. The Liberals must take responsibility for it. That is what closure should be on.
When you kill confidence, you kill the chance for investment. The Liberals, with the help of the NDP, have killed confidence in this country. That kills investment. The Liberals, with the help of the NDP, have killed investment in this country. Therefore, there are no jobs, and that is the reason.
The way the New Democratic Party has been criticizing the Conservative Party, you would think we were the government. The NDP policy and the Liberal policy are much closer together than the NDP and ours. We believe in free entreprise, fair profit, freedom of the individual and initiative. The Liberals go only part way. They do not go fast enough for the NDP. They are blood brothers with regard to their policies. When the NDP criticize the Progress Conservatives, they are trying to help their blood brothers, the Liberals.
We believe in restraint. It is necessary if we are going to fight inflation. However, this party believes in a restraint that is fair. We believe in more restraint for the rich than the poor. We believe in restraint on Ian-what's-his-name-Sinclair of the CPR and his $500,000 salary. We believe in restraint for high salaries and for our salaries, and that is why we are voting for it. However, we want restraint to be fair. We do not go along with waste and believe there should be some restraint in that area. We believe in restraint on prices.
The government is lowering and putting restraint on the wages of its own workers, but is it lowering the rents for those in Banff who face increases of 15 to 35 per cent? I ask the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) to roll back the rents of those in Banff to 5 and 6 per cent.
We ask for fairness in connection with CALEA where collective bargaining is being stopped. It goes on for the staff of ministers until April, 1983 but CALEA is going to be cut off earlier. If the government corrects that, we will see its
sincerity. There should be restraint on prices and we must do away with waste.
I want to deal with one other matter regarding this motion. The government says that Canadians want restraint only. People want restraint in all areas. They want fairness in restraint, but they are not getting it. When the government rolls back rents for those in Banff, I will say it is being fair. However, it is not being fair as long as it restrains wages to 6 per cent and 5 per cent and says that it is okay to increase rent by 15 per cent to 35 per cent. That is not fairness. It should be rolled back.
Industry is being asked to follow the government's example. The unemployed must live on a pittance compared to those of us who are working. We agree there should be restraint, but it should not be carried out on the backs of the aged and the retired people of this country. Let us not have restraint at the expense of the low-paid employees who barely get by. Let us have restraint on those in the upper brackets, such as cabinet ministers and Members of Parliament. Let us set the example. Then people will say we are doing something. That will build up confidence.
It is the free enterprise system that will bring this country back to prosperity, not socialism, whether it is fashioned by the NDP or the Liberals. That is what is killing this country. Free enterprise will give every individual confidence to invest in this country. When money is invested, jobs are created, products are manufactured and the country gets moving. What we want is productivity. We want more productivity per man per hour. If we bring that about, we will get this country out of the slump it is in. That is exactly what our leader was saying the other day. We will get the country out of its slump through free enterprise principles. Give us a chance. We challenge hon. members opposite to resign and let us show the country what can be done.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in returning to the regular debate on Bill C-124, I should like to say that many hon. members of the House have made much of the fact of the so-called principle of this bill being a principle of restraint. The principle of this bill before us is not restraint. The principle of the bill is compulsion and the transfer of wealth and power, relatively speaking, from those who do not have it, to those who have. That is wrong.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: Order, please. I apologize to the hon. member who has the floor. Would hon. members who wish to have conversations, please carry them on behind the curtains or in the lobby? The hon. member for Kootenay West.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can well appreciate why some hon. members of the House, particularly on the government side, do not want to hear anyone question the principle they say is behind this legislation. The principle is not restraint, it is compulsion, and that is all it is. We do not need to look very far to find the kind of thinking that gave rise to it. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), according to an article for Southam News written by John Ferguson on June 14, 1982, which appeared in The Vancouver Sun, made a rather inflammatory speech to the Conference Board of Canada. His speech reads in part:
Governments at all levels have gone too far, too fast, in yielding power to their unions. What we have in fact created is a series of union monopolies which have been granted power to close down large sections of our economy, to deny education to our children and hospital care to the sick, to cut off police and fire protection for the public and to bring transportation to a halt municipally, regionally and even nationally.
That is the kind of thing that gave rise to this bill. It is a feeling of revenge on the part of members opposite. They are the true heirs to Joey Smallwood.
I can remember when I first became involved in the political process. One of the debates going on at the time concerned
legislation that came down in the province of Newfoundland in 1958 or 1959 to outlaw a union from the shores of the province of Newfoundland entirely. That action was taken by a Liberal government headed by another premier and another representative of that party who could not stand to see free men and women stand up on their own two feet to challenge their kind of arbitrary dictates as to what was best for them. At that time there were loggers in the province of Newfoundland who were attempting to get a wage of $1.05 an hour, and trying to get rid of the kind of conditions that people in that industry in other parts of Canada had eliminated from their places of work decades before. At that time they hauled in their own blankets and put them down on bunks of straw or ferns in old rodent-infested bunkhouses. The Liberal premier of the province at that time decided that he could not stomach it ... that is, their reaction. He formed his own government-sponsored union and actually passed legislation which banished the union of the people's choice in that province, an action the likes of which had not been seen in this country for almost half a century. This legislation is in the same kind of spirit.
While dealing with this bill, I should like to direct a few remarks to hon. members of the official opposition. We are all well acquainted with The Globe and Mail. Most of us read it every morning. This particular newspaper is hardly a socialist one. It is not even a Liberal newspaper. If anything, it is Conservative. Every day the masthead of its editorial page reads:
The subject who is truly loyal to the Chief Magistrate will neither advise nor submit to arbitrary measures.
This was not written by Jean-Claude Parrot. It was not written by working people across this country, and particularly not by those in the public sector who see themselves singled out as victims in the public relations gimmickery of government. I talk about public relations gimmickery rather advisedly.
Earlier in the debate we reminded government members of the document entitled, "Anti-Inflation Policy, Options" which was presented to the federal cabinet some months ago. I should like to quote from that internal government document. In part it reads:
The main advantage of the program would be that it would enable the government to be seen doing something about inflation and to lay part of the blame on the private sector.
Also it reads:
We are not currently facing a wage-driven inflation such as we were in 1975;
Also it indicated that inflation had been "highly resistant to government policy, including wage and price controls."
The government has acknowledged the arguments presented in that paper. On innumerable occasions ministers of the government have expressed the same sentiments and outlined the same facts, yet we are now asked to believe that Bill
August 2, 1982

C-124, including all its amendments, will somehow do what the Anti-Inflation Board and its wage and price control mechanisms of the 1970s failed to do. At least the AIB attempted to appear to be even-handed. They do not even make that pretence this time around. Their total purpose, other than as a public relations exercise, is to attempt to bring the working people of this country to heel. This is wrong, and it is something which I and other members of my party will resist, no matter how much the Conservatives and their pals on the Liberal benches say it is time to tell workers to "git back". They make high-sounding suggestions and equity, but the kind of equity suggested by Conservatives in committee, upon which the government acted as it did with other suggestions was, "You are only discriminating against public employees; why do you not expand it to people in other industries?" They expanded upon discrimination. It was their idea of producing equity; it was funny reasoning. I have a hard time believing that they do not realize that this is no kind of equity at all. Once they get away from their haste to take a kick at the working people of this country and look at it objectively, I do not think they would believe otherwise.
Where will this kind of measure lead us? Just the other day someone brought to my attention an article that appeared in The Washington Post on July 26, 1982. It concerned an industrial dispute which was taking place in Dakota City, Nebraska. This may seem a long way away, but it well demonstrates the kind of course upon which this House appears to be embarked. There has been a strike in the meat packing industry in that city since June 7, 1982, involving some 2,400 members of the meatcutters' union. They are not on strike for higher pay; they are seeking a two year wage freeze. The company has refused to sign an agreement because it is insisting upon a four year wage freeze. During the last two months the company has brought in strikebreakers. There has been violence on the lines. A number of people have been injured and a number have been arrested. The city has become an armed camp.
This is the kind of insane violence to which such a measure leads, the kind which we saw from one end of the country to the other during the 1930s. We do not want to see it again. Surely to God they can be more enlightened in the way they deal with people.
Earlier today reference was made in the House to recent remarks of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) in a letter to the editor of one of the Toronto newspapers. At least his remarks showed an intelligent approach to labour relations. At least he understood and admitted that working people had rights, rights which are just as inviolate and just as important to the functioning of a free and democratic society as many other rights which we often proclaim in this place and in other assemblies across the land. I only wish that we had had the opportunity of having the Minister of Labour appear before us in committee. I do not know whether he was hiding or the government was keeping him hidden, but 1 am sure the government did not wish us to hear the comments which he made in his recent letter to the editor. It would not want us to hear such comments in the context of the debate in committee because the government's legislation flies in the face of those
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
kinds of principles. It flies in the face of anything akin to a free labour movement.
A few moments ago I quoted from the masthead of The Globe and Mail. Again it reads:
The subject who is truly loyal to the Chief Magistrate will neither advise nor submit to arbitrary measures.
"Arbitrary", as defined in the second edition of the Oxford Illustrated Dictionary, reads:
Derived from mere opinion, capricious; despotic; (law) discretionary.
This bill is discretionary. They have simply picked out this group to kick. They have not even attempted to appear to be even-handed. It is discriminatory, it is arbitrary. When Parliament acts in that way, how can it expect honest, hard-working people across the country who believe in freedom to respect either that law or the institution which passes it?
