speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
I am not advocating that people should disregard the law. I would be the last to do so. But, I do not think that members of this party and I are alone in understanding that, when people feel they have been subjected to laws which are discriminatory, arbitrary and capricious, many of them will react accordingly. It is a despotic law and it will be dealt with in that way. In turn, that will lead to the kind of breakdown none of us desire to see. If we are ever to begin to work together in any kind of intelligent way to put society back on the path where government, labour and management can deal with each other in good faith and in an atmosphere of trust, then we must at least respect each other's rights as individuals and as segments of society. We must deal with each other on a non-discriminatory basis.
This law could be called a "git back" law. I do not know whether hon. members are familiar with that phrase. It is used often in the American south, "Git back, boy; git back." This amendment, this new amendment of the government, is a "git back" one. It is the government's attempt to be fair. It is going to tell members of free trade unions in the country, at least those in the public sector, and in the little bit of the private sector that they arbitrarily decided to throw in with them, that if they are good boys and girls and they sit down and negotiate within the arbitrary confines of this arbitrary law, then the government, out of the goodness of its heart and acting alone, will decide, this is compensation and this is not; this is a monetary clause and that is not; and if they are all very well behaved then they will be able to negotiate within the confines of that very peculiar definition of what is monetary and what is compensatory and what is not.
There is a word for that. In the old labour lexicon it is called a yellow-dog contract, and no self respecting worker would ever sign one. That is a yellow-dog clause and this whole damned thing is a yellow-dog bill. The Norris-LaGuardia Act, passed in 1932, made the yellow-dog contract illegal. That was

August 2, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
50 years ago. I am just going to give a short example of that kind of contract. This is a typical one. It was offered by the Hitchman Coal & Coke Company to all employees in 1908 . Those who refused to sign were fired. In the case of Hitchman Coal Company v. Mitchell, the U.S. Supreme Court in 1917 declared this contract valid. In 1932 it was thrown out.
Let me quote as follows:
I am employed by and work for the Hitchman Coal and Coke Company with the express understanding that I am not a member of the United Mine Workers of America and will not become so while an employee of the Hitchman Coal and Coke Company, and that the Hitchman Coal and Coke Company is run nonunion and agrees with me that it will run non-union while I am in its employ.
If at any time while I am employed by the Hitchman Coal and Coke Company I want to become connected with the United Mine Workers of America, or any affiliated organization, I agree to withdraw from the employment of said company, and agree that while I am in the employ of that company I will not make any effort amongst its employees to bring about the unionizing of that mine against the company's wish. I have either read the above, or heard same read.
That was the yellow-dog contract that was ruled invalid by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1932, and this bill is in that same spirit. This amendment, particularly the new Clause 16, is in exactly that same spirit. As they say, 'Tse gonna be a good boy, Massa," and that is what this is all about.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: Shame, shame!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
There is a book in the province of Quebec called the "White Niggers of North America". That is not a racist term in this context. I think some members are aware of the phrase "being a good nigger" and it has nothing to do with being black or white or yellow or brown or any other colour. If you think that Canadian workers, who are used to being free people are going to say, "I'se gonna be a good boy" just because the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) over there, with his union bashing and desire to seek a servile attitude from among the employees of the Government of Canada, thinks Canadian workers are going to kowtow to that kind of attitude, then the government is very wrong.
There may be a number of Canadians, with the best of motives, who are going to get sucked in for a little while as they have been on other occasions, with regard to the War Measures Act and at other times, when this House unwisely attempted to invade the very freedom upon which this society is built. Sometimes it takes a little time for people to see very clearly exactly what is happening to some of their very basic and fundamental freedoms. But they will learn, and just as the Liberals and Conservatives voted together in that instance, the War Measures Act in 1970; just as the Liberals and Conservatives, going back further, voted together in the War Measures Act to discriminate against Japanese Canadians in the 1940s-and now they wish they had not, and everybody now says that that was a bad thing to do-and just as almost every member of this House, except for a few, maybe, who secretly keep their opinions to themselves, now says that the kind of arbitrary, dictatorial action that Joey Smallwood utilized against the International Woodworkers in the province of Newfoundland when he banished them from the shores of that
province in 1958-59-that that was wrong. In the same way, people will come to realize that this kind of legislation which is arbitrary and discriminatory is wrong as well and they will react in time against the government and against all politicians who are in a haste to find any old perceived answer to the very serious economic problems that beset our society. Those people will see through that and will punish those very shortsighted politicians accordingly; and they should.
There have been a number of comments from the other side. I have only got two or three minutes left so I will attempt to be very brief.

speechtext: Good.

speechtext:
They do not like people withdrawing their labour, they do not like free people speaking out either, and that is obvious from the tone of that remark. We do not "git back" and fit into their nice, cozy corner. I have never "got back," and I have never known the people I have worked with, people I am proud to have worked with, "git back" either. It is just not their way. We will express ourselves and we will be around, and whether it is in this place or whether it is on the street, we will be there and you will not shove us back.
There is no purpose in people having a union to protect them if that union cannot negotiate for them. The history of collective action on the part of working people is too strong and too deeply imbedded for it to be floated away and washed away by a quick flick of the wrist, as some of the people opposite would like to see happen. Unfortunately there are a few Conservative members who join with them enthusiastically in that aim. Others join them but are not quite so enthusiastic. We hope that in time they, along with the vast majority of people of this country, will some day see their way clear, in whatever forum they wish to express it, to tell this government that this action is no good, it is wrong, it has to go and they have to go too.

Mr. Speaker, I have been forced to cut my speech into two parts, the NDP having refused to give me unanimous consent to call it six o'clock at three minutes to six.
You may recall that at that time I pointed out that the NDP have, so far in recent history, voted against the UFFI bill which would give $5,000 to those unfortunates who took the government's advice to instal that insulation in their homes. They have voted against the bill before us, Bill C-124, from the beginning. This is a bill that cuts MPs' pay. They have also voted against the freedom of information bill.
Those members also talked about their voting record against the government. As I pointed out, in the 1972-74 minority government situation, the NDP voted with the Liberal government at that time 19 times before they finally voted against the government. There was another minority government in 1979 which was headed by the Conservatives. At that time the
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
NDP never once gave us the fair chance they had given the Liberals some seven years before. Not once did they support the Conservative government when it was in a minority position. They now try to claim their neutrality and dissociate themselves from the Liberals but, as the Saskatchewan election proved, they cannot get away with it.
I would like to discuss how this bill was brought about in its present form. As we all know, it was brought in as a restraint bill. The Liberal position is a rather peculiar one these days. As always, I believe that the party is being run by a combination of Mr. Goldfarb and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Mr. Goldfarb recently found out that the general public thinks that the civil servants are being paid too much, or that the public would not object to their pay being cut. Therefore, the Liberals introduced Bill C-124.
The Liberals also introduced a number of other initiatives that I believe are derived from Mr. Goldfarb's polls. They are beginning to relax on metric. Any poll could have shown them that metric is vastly unpopular in the country. So the Liberals are beginning to change their position somewhat on metric. I expect that any day they will float some kind of a vote in the House on capital punishment. That would be the ultimate in changing positions to suit Mr. Goldfarb.
I must say that the amendments to this bill are making life extremely difficult in the House. I began being a supporter of Bill C-124 because of its restraint qualities. It cut the pay of MPs, and I found it rather easy to support. However, the amendments started to come in. I find it difficult to believe that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) alone is responsible for it. Although it may seem strange, and I hate to admit it about that group of oddballs-to be kind to them let us call them that-oddballs who are running the country, if there was one member with a glimmering of sense, it was the President of the Treasury Board. But then he produced this mean, small-minded and vindictive amendment, which he brought forward. I wonder if he was forced into it by the Prime Minister. It does not suit him, yet here it is.
How did this restraint measure begin? There is a great deal of argument back and forth with various people wishing someone else to take the credit for it, but this measure started on budget night when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) brought in his budget.
As for the Minister of Finance, some people say he is the worst Minister of Finance since the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) was minister of finance. Others disagree and say he is the worst Minister of Finance since the hon. John Turner was the minister of Finance. I tend to agree with both.
In any event, the Minister of Finance said, as it appears on page 4 of what seemed to be an interminable speech that night when talking about the rollback and restraint, "However, only ministers, MPs and senators will be subject to actual cuts in pay." That suited me and received my support.

The bill was then introduced. A measure was introduced based on the provision in the budget speech about the 6 per cent limit on future pay increases. I believe that the staff around this place accepted that with very good discipline. They saw that it was necessary and beneficial and that it would help the country to become accustomed to taking less out of the public trough. They generally accepted it with a very good grace.
I have a staff of four who are all women. As the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) said, they were the ones who were treated the very worst here. Eighty per cent of the staff here-100 per cent of my staff- are women. I had an unwritten contract with my staff because they trusted me as a Member of Parliament the way I trusted the government as a Member of Parliament. I was given a global amount. In my office we decided who would get how much. They did not receive a great increase. They received this increase in April and for the last four months they have been drawing that pay because I said that that is what they could have. My staff have done their work. When they received the news that they would receive only a 6 per cent raise next year, they said, "If this is what is needed to get the country back to normal, I guess we are the goats, but we will get along with it."
The President of the Treasury Board then introduced this amendment No. 3. It is really a bombshell tucked away in the bill. The amendment would mean that those people would have to roll back 6 per cent of their pay so that they would only have had a 5 per cent increase from April. They have become accustomed to living on a certain stipend each month. They have made arrangements to pay off mortgages and to rent apartments. They have purchased new and second-hand cars. Most of them live up to their incomes. Now, bang, they are to be treated the way the Minister of Finance said that no one except ministers, MPs and senators would be subject to in terms of actual cuts in pay. This will create far more difficulties than the government imagines, but it is really noted for not realizing for a moment the consequence or consequences of its actions. It goes blindly into these half-thought-out programs and is then astonished when they do not turn out well because its helpers or advisers have said, "Do it our way and worry not."
One can never forget the look on the face of the Minister of Finance when he was questioned by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) a couple of days after his November budget. She pointed out to him that 20,000 construction workers had been laid off in the country because of the cutting off of the MURB program, the multiple unit residential building program. Builders had their allowances cut off unless a MURB had its foundation in. The result was that
20,000	people were put out of work. But the Minister of Finance had never dreamed that would happen. He had not thought through what would happen, any more than the President of the Treasury Board understood what would happen when he brought in this amendment, that he would
turn many of his friends in the House into people who are finding it extremely difficult to vote for this restraint. Yes, we are very much in favour of restraint. We are willing to accept it, even for ourselves. But it is very hard indeed to have it put on us if we must go back and tell our staff that they are to be added to that very select group which will be subject to a rollback, and that of all the 500,000 people who work for the federal government, 2,000 will have to carry the only rollback, which will be on their backs.
At page 2 of the bill, with reference to the rollback provisions, it states:
(2) This part applies to
(a) staffs of Ministers of the Crown and of members of the Senate and House
of Commons-
That affects some of our secretarial staffs. At this time it might be interesting to read just what kind of provisions we are supposed to be working under here. For the benefit of those who never do read the instructions that are sent out I would like to read from the book provided to members of the House of Commons, which is entitled "Allowances and Services". In Section 7 at page 2, under "Administration of Staff Allowance", it states:
Members of Parliament have the prerogative to recruit, hire and release employees. Rates of pay are also determined by the Member, providing such rates fall within the guidelines set out in Part B, paragraphs 2 and 3. Salary expenditures will be reflected in the member's principal budget.
Members' assistants fall under paragraphs 2 and 3 to which reference was given. The lowest level, level 1, starts at SI0,537 a year. It goes from there through to level 2, level 3 and then level 4. The salary at the very top of level 4 is $25,408. However, members are given a global budget, and, as it is stated, salaries are at our discretion. It is just as plain as can be. I expect that if this bill passes, this whole manual will be scrubbed out and we will be put on a new footing. One of the parts of the new footing is that our own staff would probably never believe us again.
With reference to classification and salary, it is quite interesting. This book of instruction for MPs states:
As it is the prerogative of the member to determine the rate of pay of an employee, it is also the responsibility of the member to initiate any change in the rate of pay of an employee. Only the signature of the Member may authorize the appointment, the amendment to the rate of pay, or the termination of employment in either the Ottawa parliamentary office or the constituency office.
It is really something like the limit put on the indexation of retired servicemen. I am doubtful as to whether the government has the authority to break these contracts. If it happened in the private sector, I suspect that a firm would be sued for the money which is still outstanding or due to the employee, because there was a verbal contract, at least with the staff. It can be backed up by papers sent out by the parliamentary administration which lists everyone and states what they are paid. Suddenly, this contract has no bearing or effect. It is not a contract. It seems wrong to me.
The fat really hit the fire when word came out just after the budget, which I believe was June 28, that the exempt staff of the ministers had received a pay raise of 11 per cent some 11

days before the budget. The members of the House of Commons were asked to put their usual intelligence on hold and believe that the government knew nothing about the matter, that the President of the Treasury Board knew nothing about it and that no one knew what was in the budget until budget night. What the government said about the November budget was that no one knew what was in it, including the Minister of Finance, until budget night.

Yes, some people wonder whether he knows anything about what was in it to this day.
There was a press report that this was the second of a pair of pay raises. I have only seen it once. It is by no means conclusive. I would look forward to the President of the Treasury Board telling me truthfully at some time whether or not there was another pay raise involved before that. For those who do not know about exempt staff, "exempt staff' means employees who are exempt from having their pay questioned, and the government takes very good care not to tell us how much they get paid, no matter how much they get paid. So we have to take the government's word about whether there was or was not a previous pay raise. It seems to me that is partly the fault of the Liberal backbenchers more than those in the opposition whose job it is to oppose, but I understand that members of cabinet received quite a bit of criticism about raising the salaries of their own exempt staff just 11 days before a budget was introduced, which limited to 6 per cent the increase for the staff of everyone else and left theirs at 11 per cent. This seemed to be a sly trick to get in a pay raise quietly just before the ceiling was put on.
Not only did the opposition oppose it, but I also believe that some hon. members, the more forthright of the backbenchers in the Liberals, criticized the cabinet, not realizing how dangerous it is for any backbencher to criticize the cabinet. The reaction was swift and immediate and their staff will now have their salaries rolled back. In my opinion, this is absolutely outrageous, and is the reaction of a petulant, vindictive man, and a meaner example of the use of power is really hard to contemplate. That is why at the beginning of my remarks I said that I am amazed if it really came from the President of the Treasury Board, although he is a friend of the Prime Minister and has never before, as far as I know, participated in any actions similar to this. I know, of course, how I will vote on Amendment No. 3, which relates to this matter.

Is it because of civil servants' wages being too high that close to 50,000 auto workers are not working?

I know that there have been a lot of comments and a great deal of commentary about ministers' staffs and the salaries and perks that they enjoy. Something has gone wrong. my staff have not gone home, I send them home. spoken out both in debate and in committee as being adamantly opposed to the bill in general. We are certainly opposed to amendments that will curtail the increase which the staff got about four months ago. This amendment will affect our staff members severely.

What this bill has done for me and for many members of the public service as well as members of any labour union is to indicate the extent to which the Liberal government-and we will see the proof of this when the votes are counted-and to what extent Liberal members will go in order to gain favour in this land. The cynical attitude of Canadians toward their federal government will be totally justified.
Bill C-124 simply confirms the kind of attitude and cynicism which exists toward the government. We have a government which has ruled the land during most of the last 117 years. Basically it controls its policies through Gallup and public polls.
The situation we have today is a government which is in disarray and is disorganized. It is unaware of where it is going. The feeling exists in the land that pubic servants are doing well in comparison with many other unions and businesses in the country. Canadians are looking for answers. The Liberal government is prepared to give a simplistic answer, that it is public servants who are too rich, whose compensation packages are too rich. The government will give the public something which it perceives will gain some political favour, that is, control over public sector wages. We have a government with a 6-5 formula-the mythical 6 per cent society-which the government is prepared to use and impose upon public servants in an attempt to gain favour in the business community and with the electorate who really do not understand the economic problems which have led to the present situation in Canada.
We have a government which is willing to say to Canadians that it should set a precedent by controlling the public service to a 6 per cent increase this year and to a 5 per cent one next year and that somehow this will solve most of the economic problems in Canada. We know that is not true. Public servants know that is not true. Trade unions know that is not true. Deep down, most Canadians know that it will not be the salvation of the Canadian economy.
In terms of the public service and its members, they are in somewhat of a state of shock. They know that there are some critical problems in the Canadian economy. They have heard over and over again that the public service somehow, in some mythical way, is to blame for them. They are quite willing in some ways to carry their share of the load of economic recovery. They have not reacted to the extent to which they will react when they discover what is being imposed upon them in

Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
terms, not only of salary curtailment but, more important, what they have lost in terms of their ability to bargain collectively with their employer.
I come from a constituency which is very heavily trade union oriented, mostly in the forest industry. I am interested in seeing the reaction of the unemployed workers in my riding toward the government program in Bill C-124. This program gets at the public service. I think there is a sense within Canada-and certainly within the private trade union movement in my riding-that this bill will not stop at the public sector. It is a propaganda ploy of the government in order to curtail collective bargaining in many other sectors. To some extent it has already included the independent trade union movement within areas in which Crown corporations are involved through contracts. IWA and the Canadian paper-workers' union in my riding have nearly 10,000 members. They are looking very carefully at the bill and at the possibility that come this fall, when they have seen a total failure of the bill to bring any reduction in the cost of living or to make available any greater employment, they will be fighting the Liberal government on the same kinds of programs with which public servants have found themselves faced at the moment.
There are approximately 6,000 members of the IWA in Port Alberni. Approximately 600 of them are currently employed. We have pulp mills which will be shut down for 11 weeks over the summer months and into September. We have sawmills which are closed down. We have loggers out of work. Only 600 of the 6,000 are working in that valley. Many of these people have been unemployed for 11 months now. They are looking at the spectre of going on unemployment insurance within the next month or two, which will bring the total in the community to approximately 1,000 workers on unemployment insurance and then on to welfare.
I ask these people what this bill means to them. Do they think this bill will put any people back to work in the forest industry? Obviously the answer is no. The reduction in incomes of public servants across Canada will mean a reduction in expenditures by union members within their local communities. Local business people are already suffering. There are record bankruptcies in the small business sector of Canada. Those businesses will have even less money. As long as the government persists in a high interest rate policy, home owners will be unable to meet their mortgage payments. New home owners and young people seeking new homes will be unable even to think about purchasing them.
Woodworkers in Nanaimo, Campbell River, Duncan, Kamloops and Prince George will continue on unemployment insurance. Also they will continue to face the spectre of even worse fate, that is, the welfare rolls.
We wonder how such a bill ever got this far in a country which prides itself on freedom, the right of self-expression, the right to a job and free movement across the land. Most Canadians feel very fortunate about living in Canada, considering the difficulties in most other nations. In a land which prides itself on its democratic system and the choice to make a free decision at election time as to what government the citizens want to represent them, the government has recently
gone through a very difficult time in adopting a new Constitution. It took pride in its Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Yet, within a matter of months it comes along and says to public servants that for a period of two years they no longer have the right to collective bargaining nor the right to deal with health and safety issues. It tells them that their current contracts will be frozen and that the wages which they will negotiate over the next two years will be limited to 6 per cent and 5 per cent, regardless of the cost of living, the price of housing or of fuel.
A government which will impose this kind of legislation on its public servants, who have been loyal to it and to the Canadian public, will carry the process even further. It will take away freedoms from all of us, whether they are rights in the trade union movement or the right of small business people to make decisions on how they will run their businesses. It seems to me that the government, through this bill, is quite prepared to go to any extent.
In talking to people in the public service in my riding-and I think the situation is probably similar across the land-I found in them a hesitancy to take strong and deliberate action against the bill. I think that is a reflection of the dedication and commitment of public servants, not only in the federal government sector but also in the provincial area. People working for governments really feel some commitment to their jobs, to their ministers and to their departments. This bill simply cuts all the respect they may have felt for the government. I suspect that it will lead to the kind of attitude which many public servants felt when the Conservatives campaigned in 1979. In order to gain political favour across Canada, the Conservative government talked about 60,000 fewer public servants. It did not really explain from where they would be cut, from what departments or programs. It talked a little about them being lost through attrition, but not about how it would affect programs which were built up by government over the years. Whether social programs or economic programs for the business community, we were simply going to curtail about 2 per cent of the public service in each department and we were going to reduce that heavy, overweight public service by 60,000 people, the same kind of effect that the Conservatives are now talking about in terms of slashing the federal budget. There were no specifics in it, simply that we are going to have to slash budgets and we are going to have to turf out some of the public service.
Again I think of my riding, of the number of people unemployed and how this bill is going to affect them. It is not going to put any of them to work; it is not going to give them any more confidence in this government; it is not going to give anybody any confidence in this government. I think that most people, when they assess this bill, will recognize it is simply a political ploy to give the impression at the end of this session that the government has finally recognized that we have an economic problem, and their knee-jerk reaction to this problem is again to attack the public service. If this does not work and we get into the session in October and we still have an inflation

rate of 11 per cent, an unemployment rate nearing 11 per cent or 12 per cent, budgets for provincial and municipal governments for welfare skyrocketing, and a lack of any industrial strategy in Canada, this government very likely will be prepared to bring in wage and price controls, or at least wage controls in the private sector.
We went through 1975, did we not? We went through 1974 when this government was attempting to get re-elected and it condemned the wage and price controls advocated by the Conservative leader, Mr. Stanfield, at that time, and soon after they were back in. We had an economic crisis in Canada, and the only solution to that of course was wage and price controls. Workers' salaries and workers' income have really never recovered from the 1975 era. He said: Mr. Speaker, I would first like to explain what the effect of this amendment might be. It would be to delete Section 4 which was proposed by the government in the present bill. It says:
(4) This Part applies to employees of Canadian Pacific Limited and its subsidiaries who are employed in the operation of a railway and to the employees of the following:
(a)	Ontario Northland Railway;
(b)	Algoma Central Railway Company;
(c)	Toronto Terminals Railway Company;

That clause was not there when this bill first came to the House of Commons. We were told by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) that this was a bill which would specifically apply to Crown corporations and government employees. We were told that it did not apply to the private sector. The inclusion of this amendment has now brought in the private sector.
This amendment was included after all groups who were entitled to present witnesses to the committee had done so. In other words, no further witnesses were heard after this amendment was placed before the committee.
Of course, this meant that the railway unions and others who were concerned about the effect of this amendment, not only on collective bargaining but also on railway transportation, especially in western Canada, were not given an opportunity to be heard.
Many of us, especially those of us who live in western Canada, believe that the long term effect of this amendment will be to bring the railway peace which has existed in this country for the last number of years to an end. We believe that by singling out the railway industry as the only private sector industry to come under the auspices of this bill, the government will have brought about the prejudice, hate and longterm instability that it said it did not want to create in this country.
The Liberal majority on that committee refused to allow those people who were concerned about this amendment to come before the committee. Members of all parties were not able to hear what those concerned groups of Canadians felt about this amendment.

I suggested earlier today that this indecent haste showed a lack of a concern for the importance of this bill, an extremely important bill. This bill allows the government to break contracts that it has already signed. It changes the

speechtext:
While my colleague said we heard from Ian Sinclair, that is not quite true. Those of us who served on the committee did not hear from him. We did ask that Ian Sinclair, who is head of Canadian Pacific investments and is a leader in the private sector calling for wage controls, appear before the committee. He indicated to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance that this is the route that they should follow. As well, he told the press that he was in favour of voluntary controls. The next day, the government did not bring in voluntary controls for CP, it brought in mandatory controls. As a result, Ian Sinclair, who is telling Inco to restrict the wages of its workers to 6 per cent and 5 per cent, Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting to restrict the wages of their workers to 6 per cent and 5 per cent, telling some of the wood and forestry companies to keep their workers' wages down to 6 per cent and 5 per cent, no longer has to worry about it himself. As far as the railways are concerned, the government has sent Mr. Sinclair a thank you note by automatically holding those workers' wages to 6 per cent and 5 per cent.
We have an ironic situation because the NDP members on the miscellaneous estimates committee which investigated this bill moved a motion to ask Ian Sinclair, who is leading the
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
private sector crusade on this issue, to come to the committee to give evidence, as others were invited to do. However, the Liberal majority on that committee voted it down. Mr. Sinclair has met at least twice with the Prime Minister behind closed doors. He advocated the bill that is before us. He went to the press, to the private sector and to employers, saying why this bill is such a great deal, such a great suggestion for the future of Canada. But we, as Members of Parliament, who were supposed to study the bill clause by clause, and to make amendments and improvements where possible, were not allowed to hear what that man had to say. It is interesting because, after all, witnesses had been heard by that committee, and after the government refused to hear any more witnesses, we then received this amendment. Of course, the workers and communities that are affected could not make their presentations.
There was someone else who could not make presentations. That was the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia). As we have pointed out in some previous debate, workers such as the Canadian Pacific workers do not come under the jurisdiction of the President of the Treasury Board; those workers come under the Canada Labour Code. That means that we are in a situation where it is not the responsibility of the President of the Treasury Board to pass legislation or to make suggestions about workers under the Canada Labour Code. It is the responsibility of the Minister of Labour.
Earlier today I read a letter written by the Minister of Labour to The Globe and Mail wherein he defended the right to strike and the collective bargaining process. As well, he mentioned that the Parliament of Canada had made Labour Canada responsible for the operation of companies like Canadian Pacific and others which come under the private sector. In other words, he said, "That is my area. I have certain views in this area and I am the minister responsible." We agree with the minister. He is responsible to the House and to Canadians.
The hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) asked that the minister come before the committee. The first time, the government members said, "Okay, he can come." But they said he had to come at 3.30 p.m. the following Monday. It appeared that the Minister of Labour could not come at that time on Monday. We could accept that. It is reasonable to assume that a minister, just like any other Member of Parliament, has some other duties that he or she must look after. When the committee met again, we said, "Okay, we still want him. When can we get him? Can we get him to appear before the committee?" Again, the Liberal majority on that committee said, "No, we do not want him to appear before the committee. No, we will not invite him to appear before the committee." That decision was made ten minutes prior to the introduction of this amendment by the government. Ten minutes after the Liberal majority on that

August 2, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
committee had said the Minister of Labour could not appear before the committee to give evidence, to explain his position and how he thought the bill would affect the workers who come under his responsibility, the President of the Treasury Board circulated an amendment in that committee saying that Canadian Pacific would be excluded in the legislation. How in God's name or anyone else's name could the committee be perceived to be hearing witnesses? How could the committee be perceived as studying the legislation clause by clause, which is the function of a committee as we well know? How could we be perceived to be looking after the interests of the public if the Liberal majority in that committee strangled debate, prevented witnesses from appearing, and then introduced very important amendments after the last witness has been heard? Of course, the answer is that we could not.
Not only did we have to act without the knowledge of the Minister of Labour, but also without the knowledge that may have been given to us by his mediation officers. We also had to vote yea or nay to government and opposition amendments without knowing what the deputy minister of labour thought. We had to act without knowing what the labour relations officers thought. We were in the situation where we had to act without the knowledge of the people who serve the country in the Department of Labour, the people we rely on to ensure that negotiations are proceeding, to ensure that labour laws are fair and, once passed by government, are actually followed up on or pursued.
I have not been in Parliament very long. I was elected in 1979. But after having served on five or six committees, I can say I have never yet been told that the minister or his senior officials could not appear before a committee, except for that time a week and a half ago. That was unheard of to me. Other hon. members who have been here longer may know of other times when this has happened, but I find it to be more than remarkable; I find it to be repugnant.
We took that matter very seriously. When the Liberal majority on the committee refused to hear the Minister of Labour, my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) walked out. He may have a chance to speak later on in this debate, even though time allocation has been brought in-

In the last few days, we have said much concerning this bill and we will be saying more over the next day or two allotted for this debate. The government has preached in the House that it is in favour of co-operation. It
has said that if we are to get Canada out of the current economic slump, then all sectors, whether the provincial government employees, the public sector or private sector employees or the municipal employees, must all co-operate and work together, and that if we do not work together we will really not be able to solve the problems that we face. As one of the members who spoke previously said, it is not simply a matter of wage controls. It involves all those factors. The whole history of this bill and this amendment is typical of that approach. The day after the President of the Treasury Board announced the bill, he did meet with the Public Service Alliance for 30 minutes, before rushing off to some other meeting. However, he did not meet with them prior to this bill being talked about in the June 28 budget. He did not meet with the Public Service Alliance. For a number of years we in the New Democratic Party have said that the economy is in trouble, that there must be some kind of cooperative approach. We believe that. My colleague, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) pointed out a number of areas where the government has not had very good control over the coffers it is entrusted to look after. speechtext: I thought you said in or out.

speechtext:
Definitely out. We argued that position in committee and in the House of Commons.
I talked about labour peace. I would like to talk about the fact that in many ways Canadian National has been treated as if it were a private corporation. It was not an attempt by this government to get into the railway business when it took over the company that formed Canadian National. We took over two private sector companies that has basically mismanaged their affairs. It was felt there was a need for the Government of Canada to move in this area.
We believe this has basically been treated as a private sector area and so we must keep those unions out of this program. We have made specific recommendations to that effect. We are also concerned about whether the action by the government is legal, but that will be dealt with in a different court. Parliament for the most part is not a court.
I am concerned about another aspect of bringing in Canadian Pacific at this time. Both Canadian Pacific and Canadian National have signed contracts with their workers. The effect of bringing those workers under the provisions of this bill will be to break those collective agreements.
Private sector and public sector companies have signed agreements with their workers, but all of a sudden Canadian National-and even more suddenly Canadian Pacific-have come come under the auspices of this bill. That means signed collective agreements are broken. As I said, the government has said it does not care if workers and their railway companies have signed a collective agreement for the next couple of years. The government does not care that it knew what was going on, through its arm's length relationship with Canadian National, and that it as the Government of Canada okayed Canadian National's agreement with its workers. Despite the fact that there is a collective agreement signed by both sides- a number of parties were involved-and despite the fact that the agreement was signed in good faith, the government has decided that means nothing. The government has listened to Ian Sinclair and a few of his "poorly paid" buddies, the barefoot boys from Bay Street. Ian Sinclair's income is $550,000 a year, and we are not sure about the extras he might get. I suspect he may even have a railway pass. Mr. de Grand-pre receives a salary from Bell Canada of $650,000 a year. He is another poverty striken lad. After listening to Mr. Sinclair and Mr. de Grandpre in the back rooms, the government has decided that the contract between the railways and their workers is no longer worth very much. Because of its majority in the House of Commons the government will force this bill through the House. The contract between the railways and their workers will be rolled back, and another contract cannot be negotiated unless, according to Motion No. 17:

speechtext: The divine right of Liberals.

Yes, I agree that the workers affected by this bill are being sacrificed.
The government's new argument is that it will still allow collective bargaining. Hon. members opposite say, "Don't worry about this bill, folks." Last Thursday there was a press release put out in the name of the President of the Treasury Board. It fooled a few people in this House because it said: "Hey, guess what! You can negotiate again." We believe the government basically acts as the elective arm of the Gallup poll. We cannot trust this government with an amendment which says that the governor in council may, by order, terminate the application of this act, because it says nothing about how the government will make that decision. The amendment does not say that if the government thinks it is for the good of the country it will let people negotiate. The amendment does not say that a group, which is behind because its agreements over the last five or six years have not kept up with the cost of living, may negotiate. The amendment does not say that the government will decide on the basis of any empirical facts or even government goals or objectives that it will allow negotiations to continue. The amendment just says "the governor in council may", with absolutely no regulations, specifications or indications of what the government will do. We do not trust the government with this power, and one of the functions we will perform as we go through this debate in the House is to point out matters like the inclusion of Canadian Pacific and why we believe the bill has to be amended so that we do not have to leave everything up to this government amendment, which is the whole bill, because that basically is what is happening. We will be coming to this catch-all amendment at some time before the final vote and, I suspect, because of the nature of the closure motion, we will not have an opportunity to debate it in this House. The amendment really says that everything the government spent the last month on may be null and void, if the government so determines.
The debate has to take place, not on that final clause because we will never get to it, but on each and every clause as we go through them. We have proposed that the government amendment bringing in Canadian Pacific must be removed and I have stated the reasons for that.
I realize that it is ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker, but this is my last chance to speak on this matter. We are not out to kill the Canadian economy; we are out to make sure that if we have a bill-whether we like the bill or not-it is the best possible one that we can have for government, business and for all Canadians. Because of that, we do not want what I called earlier a namby-pamby bill, all loopholes and with no direction to help the unemployed, private businessmen, farmers or any other group of Canadians concerned about the economy of the country.

subtopic: AIRPORTS-INQUIRY RESPECTING GOVERNMENT'S INTENTIONS TO MAKE MIRABEL PROFITABLE
AIRPORTS-INQUIRY RESPECTING GOVERNMENT'S INTENTIONS TO MAKE MIRABEL PROFITABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is probably the last time in this session that I will have an opportunity to ask the minister about a subject that is of special interest, not only to the riding of Argenteuil-Papineau but also to my colleagues from the ridings of Laval, Duvernay, Blainville-Deux-Montagnes, Terrebonne, Labelle and to the entire population of the Lower Laurentians, the North Shore, Montreal and the Laurentians. I am speaking on behalf of some 3,000 employees now working at Mirabel who are faced with an uncertain future. I am speaking on behalf of the municipalities on the North Shore that are trying to develop and plan their development in terms of the airport that was built at Mirabel and which was supposed to be the gateway to North America. Mr. Speaker, on April 21, 1980, I rose in the House to ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) for a decision to lift restrictions on development at Mirabel. The minister answered that a study would be ready by June, 1980. On December 2, 1980, 1 questioned the minister again, and mentioned development at the airports of Malton, Calgary and Edmonton, and asked him what he was doing to make Mirabel a profitable enterprise. The answer was that an announcement was forthcoming. On February 18, 1981, I rose again in the House to ask the minister about Mirabel. After further delay another answer. On March 23, 1981, I asked the minister once again about making Mirabel a profitable entreprise. This time, his parliamentary secretary gave me a list of measures aimed at encouraging the use of Mirabel, an old list that was published when the airport opened.
On April 23, 1981, 1 questioned the minister once again, this time about the cost of fuel used at Mirabel, and I asked him what he intended to do about the situation. Once more, I got an evasive answer. On October 26, 1981, 1 was still asking the minister questions. On February 16, 1982, 33 mayors from the North Shore area and some 80 councillors were present in the House. My questions were about flight transfers and again, how Mirabel could be made profitable. The minister answered as usual, but this time he was a little more specific and said that a decision would be made within the next two or three months. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, the minister's answer was given on February 16, 1982. On May 14, in other words, two days before the end of the period specified by the minister, I asked whether the government would shortly be tabling a document or a study showing that a policy decision would be made with a view to making Mirabel profitable. The answer was that the
Adjournment Debate
government hoped to make good its promise made on February 16, 1982.
On May 20, 1982, I rose in the House again, Mr. Speaker, and as always, not for my own benefit but on behalf of people who are waiting for a decision and for the benefit of 3,000 employees faced with an uncertain future. The answer was that the government hoped to make the right decision and that it was a delicate matter. On July 16 of this year, there were rumours from usually well-informed sources that the minister, urged by some of his officials, had submitted to cabinet a document recommending the shutdown of one of the runways at Mirabel. I rose in the House and asked a question that probably sounded a bit ludicrous, namely, whether the minister wanted to shut down the take-off runway or the landing runway.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I would like an answer to that question because the plan recommended by the Department of Transport is unacceptable to the people of the North Shore and to their Member of Parliament.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-(A) APPLICATION FOR PASSPORTS. (B) REQUEST THAT APPLICATION FORM BE REDESIGNED
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-(A) APPLICATION FOR PASSPORTS. (B) REQUEST THAT APPLICATION FORM BE REDESIGNED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I hope I get as sympathetic and as encouraging a reply to my question as did the hon. member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mr. Gourd) from the parliamentary secretary. At the same time, I hope it is a little more enlightening than the answer he just received.
Some time ago, I rose in my place in the House to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) why it is necessary for Canadian citizens when applying for a passport to include information as to their birth place on their
19940

August 2, 1982
Adjournment Debate
passport application. I was not so concerned about information on the application form itself, but rather on the actual passport document. The reason is that we have many, many citizens in Canada whose birth place is behind the Iron Curtain.
I am sure many members realize that Iron Curtain countries, particularly countries such as Czechoslovakia, and I expect East Germany, the German Democratic Republic, Poland and other east bloc countries, do not recognize the validity of exit from those countries without an exit visa. People leaving countries, such as Czechoslovakia, are deemed to have committed a criminal offence simply by leaving the country. This means when former citizens want to return to visit their birth place, or relatives in Czechoslovakia, for example, they are deemed to be fugitives from justice and liable to arrest. In addition, if they received any kind of education in the country of their birthplace, that education is deemed to be part of the public expense for which former citizens are liable.
Since Canada extends dual citizenship to its citizens, regardless of birthplace, this means we accept the citizenship within Canada of that person as well as citizenship of another country. However, in the case of Iron Curtain countries, those countries refuse to yield that former citizenship to the new Canadian citizen and, therefore, the Canadian citizen has an unwilling dual citizenship even though he would like to renounce the former citizenship of an east bloc country. That puts him in a very precarious position.
I would think that the Department of External Affairs would be ingenious enough to be able to handle this. Surely the commitment we have to international standards for application forms and to international standards for passports does not reach into that particular sphere where we jeopardize the security of our own citizens when they visit foreign countries. I can imagine a Canadian citizen taking his Canadian passport, going to Checkpoint Charlie, seeing the officer at Checkpoint Charlie or at the boundary of Czechoslovakia, having that officer look at his Canadian passport and seeing his birthplace, whatever it might be, a city such as-

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-(A) APPLICATION FOR PASSPORTS. (B) REQUEST THAT APPLICATION FORM BE REDESIGNED
speechtext: Dresden.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-(A) APPLICATION FOR PASSPORTS. (B) REQUEST THAT APPLICATION FORM BE REDESIGNED
speechtext:
-Dresden, East Germany, or Prague, Czechoslovakia. Immediately that officer says, "Aha, a citizen of my country. I wonder if he has paid his indebtedness for his citizenship. I wonder if he is draftable into the armed forces. 1 wonder if he has paid for the criminal offence of leaving this country." It seems to me that Canadian citizens, once Canada has accepted them as citizens, ought to enjoy all rights and privileges which are ours as Canadian citizens. One of these rights is security.
Games area already being played at border crossing points. I talked to a gentleman just a week ago; as a matter of fact, an airline pilot. He told me that when he was in Europe he had a special passport. When he was going to visit Yugoslavia, all of a sudden, because the border crossing guard saw that he was
nervous about his special passport and what it might implicate him in, the border guard slipped a piece of paper into the passport and stamped it, so that the passport itself would not be disfigured with a Yugoslavian stamp.
We all know it is difficult to enter an Arab country if one's passport is stamped with an Israeli stamp. Going the other way there is no problem, so the Israelis gladly put a piece of paper into the passport and allow the guard at the border crossing simply to stamp the piece of paper, not jeopardizing that citizen's right or opportunity to enter an Arab country. These kinds of games are being played. We all understand that.
Why is it so difficult for the Department of External Affairs to make one small concession in passports, by simply deleting the blank on the passport which indicates where the person was born? Then we could enjoy all the rights and protections which ought to be ours as Canadian citizens when we visit foreign countries. Why should a citizen from Czechoslovakia, Roumania, Bulgaria or the Democratic Republic of Germany; why should a citizen of Canada, because he was born in one of the east bloc countries, have to stay home and deny himself the opportunity of visiting his relatives because he is afraid of what will happen to him if he goes there? Why should he be fearful as he crosses the border at Checkpoint Charlie to go into that country? It seems to me that the Department of External Affairs could make that one small concession and give Canadian citizens the full rights of citizenship when they get their passports.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman Kelly (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-(A) APPLICATION FOR PASSPORTS. (B) REQUEST THAT APPLICATION FORM BE REDESIGNED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the place of birth is requested in the prescribed application form for a passport in order to assist in the identification of the applicant, by verifying the information provided with the documentation submitted to confirm identity, proof of citizenship and, therefore, entitlement to a Canadian passport.
Canadian passports are issued to fulfil the requirements of present day travel and to give evidence of the Canadian citizenship of the bearer. They do not reflect any other nationality. This practice is designed to avoid involving the passport in any political controversy while maintaining its viability as a travel document which will permit Canadians to travel in all parts of the world.
The policy of the Department of External Affairs has been to include place of birth in passports. It is included by tradition and international custom as it is a very important element of identification since, unlike the physical description, it is unchangeable and cannot be altered.
The fact that the passport meets international norms and provides full identifying information is of benefit to all Canadians for a number of reasons. Provision of the place of birth in the passport obviates for the majority of travelling Canadians further questioning by foreign officials examining them as to their identity. It has a bearing on the negotiation with other

August 2, 1982

countries of reciprocal visa waiving agreements, as the information is of primary importance when obtaining permission to enter a foreign country. The place of birth in the passport must agree with the place of birth given in the visa application.
Place of birth information is also a requirement of the Canadian government for persons seeking to obtain a visa to enter Canada. As we require this information of visitors to Canada, to omit it from the Canadian passport, where it may be equally an entry requirement of the other country, would derogate from the concept of reciprocity and would ultimately handicap Canadian travellers generally.

subtopic: RAILWAYS-(A) EFFECT OF WAGE CONTROLS ON CANADIAN PACIFIC AGREEMENTS. (B) TIMING OF IMPOSITION
RAILWAYS-(A) EFFECT OF WAGE CONTROLS ON CANADIAN PACIFIC AGREEMENTS. (B) TIMING OF IMPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 30, 1982, I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) whether or not the government had carefully thought through all the implications of Bill C-124, the bill to limit wage increases in the public sector to 6 per cent and 5 per cent. 1 asked the President of the Treasury Board whether they had considered the effects their program would have on collective bargaining in the railway sector, by including the CNR in its wage control program. The CNR and the CPR bargain together with the railway unions and the concern expressed by the railway unions, among others, was that the historical accomplishment of joint bargaining between the railways and the railway unions would be jeopardized. The concern was expressed that the pieces would never be able to be put back together again.
There was a simple solution to this problem and that was to take the CNR out of the wage control program. This is what I advocated in committee when we were discussing Bill C-124 with the Canadian Railway Labour Association which were before us to make sure the government knew the full implications of what it was doing. The association was concerned about the attack on collective bargaining in general which Bill C-124 represents, about the way it breaks already signed contracts and about the way it limits collective bargaining on non-monetary as well as monetary matters.
What was the government's response? The response of the government was to make matters worse, to compound the injustice for thousands of Canadians by bringing the CPR in under the program and giving the government another beachhead in the private sector for the day when it brings in full wage controls.
The bill to control wages in the public sector is an incompetent, cowardly and unjust response to Canada's admittedly serious economic problems. It takes advantage of the willingness of the average Canadian to help out his country and to do his bit for the economy. The Liberals and the Tories are more willing to take advantage of this virtue in our people, than to show any virtue of their own by facing up to the real causes of inflation. To do this would require courage to stand up to the banks, stand up to the multinationals, stand up to the Americans and to stand up to the values and perceptions of the investment and business communities which are the lifeline
Adjournment Debate
and real centre of both the Liberal Party and the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada.
The Conservatives often like to say of the NDP that we are in bed with the Liberals. They do not have the capacity to develop an intelligent critique of our policies or, for that matter, to develop any policies of their own. All they know how to do, in their fear of the NDP, is to go around western Canada, in particular, slandering the good name of the NDP by falsely associating us with the Liberal Party.
The facts speak for themselves. The Conservatives have voted with the Liberal government in this Parliament twice as often as has the NDP, and those occasions have always been the same in nature. They have always been votes in which there was a choice to be made between the interests of average Canadians and the interests of the powerful and wealthy in this country. When it comes to that kind of a choice, there is no difference between the Liberals and the Conservatives. The Liberal-Conservative coalition is the most basic coalition in Canada. Bill C-124 is just the latest example of it.
The NDP, and the CCF before it, was formed to challenge this oppressive illusion that there is really a choice between the Liberals and the Conservatives. Let Bill C-124 stand as an illustration of our point.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman Kelly (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: RAILWAYS-(A) EFFECT OF WAGE CONTROLS ON CANADIAN PACIFIC AGREEMENTS. (B) TIMING OF IMPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier this year Canadian Pacific Limited, Canadian National Railways and several smaller railways signed a master agreement with a number of unions respresenting their non-operating employees. The master agreement, dated April 26, 1982, is for a two year period commencing January 1, 1982. The agreement provides for wage increases of 12 per cent on January 1, 1982, 9 per cent on January 1, 1983 and contains a COLA clause.
Following the introduction of Bill C-124 representations and information were received from the companies involved, the unions concerned and others. After giving full consideration, an amendment was introduced to Clause 3 of Bill C-124 which would extend coverage to the railways operated by Canadian Pacific Limited and the other smaller railways which are signatories to the master agreement.
Bill C-124 will permit the negotiated terms and conditions to stand until the first wage rate following June 29, 1982, comes into effect; namely January 1, 1983. The 9 per cent increase negotiated for January 1, 1983, will become 6 per cent under the program until December 31, 1983, and 5 per cent on January 1, 1984, to last until December 31, 1984.
The inclusion of CP employees under the bill will ensure the maintenance of the long standing pattern of negotiations with CP and CN. Canadian National and Canadian Pacific have jointly negotiated their labour agreements since immediately following the removal of wage and price controls after the Second World War. With some groups, joint railway negotiations actually go back to the First World War.

August 2, 1982
Adjournment Debate
Recognizing this historical relationship, the proposals will ensure that employees of CN are treated in a way no less favourable than the employees of CP. Not to have included CP under the bill would have destroyed the relationship at the end of 1983, when CP would have been faced with renewed labour negotiations while CN would still have one year to go under the program.
Thus, the proposed legislation results in equitable application in the railway industry and eliminates an unfair imbalance
that may have developed between the competing Crown corporations and private sector corporations.
